For every claim, show its number, linked policy number, claim amount and percentage contribution to that policy's total claim amount. Round percentages to two decimal places; leave the percentage empty when the total is zero. Arrange by policy number and then claim number. Include all claim types and statuses and use the values as recorded.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will divide each claims amount by the total amount within its policy id partition.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); insurance_products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); policies(policy_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, start_date, status, premium_amount); claims(claim_id PK, policy_id FK, claim_date, claim_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT claim_id,policy_id,amount,ROUND(100.0*amount/NULLIF(SUM(amount) OVER(PARTITION BY policy_id),0),2) record_percent FROM claims ORDER BY policy_id,claim_id;

business_scenario:
An insurance service manager wants to prepare a summary for each group. The team has records of customers, policies and claims.

Add the premium amount across each customer's policies, including all statuses. Within each customer group, select the one with the largest total. Break ties by choosing the smaller customer number. Show their number, name, group and total. Exclude customers without policies, and arrange the groups alphabetically.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will join customers and policies to total premium amount for every customers and segment. I will row-number within each segment and keep rank 1.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); insurance_products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); policies(policy_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, start_date, status, premium_amount); claims(claim_id PK, policy_id FK, claim_date, claim_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: WITH totals AS (SELECT m.customer_id,m.customer_name,m.segment,SUM(r.premium_amount) total_amount FROM customers m JOIN policies r ON m.customer_id=r.customer_id GROUP BY m.customer_id,m.customer_name,m.segment), ranked AS (SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY segment ORDER BY total_amount DESC,customer_id) rn FROM totals) SELECT customer_id,customer_name,segment,total_amount FROM ranked WHERE rn=1 ORDER BY segment;

business_scenario:
An insurance service manager wants to identify records needing a closer look. The team has records of customers, policies and claims.

Find claims whose claim amount is above the average for all claims belonging to the same policy. Include the current claim when calculating that average. Show the claim number, policy number and value. Exclude values equal to the average. Arrange by policy number and then value highest first. Include all claim types and statuses and use the values as recorded.

answer_sql: SELECT claim_id,policy_id,amount FROM claims e WHERE amount>(SELECT AVG(x.amount) FROM claims x WHERE x.policy_id=e.policy_id) ORDER BY policy_id,amount DESC;

answer_sql: WITH counts AS (SELECT m.customer_id,m.customer_name,COUNT(r.policy_id) record_count FROM customers m LEFT JOIN policies r ON m.customer_id=r.customer_id GROUP BY m.customer_id,m.customer_name) SELECT customer_id,customer_name,record_count FROM counts WHERE record_count>(SELECT AVG(record_count) FROM counts) ORDER BY record_count DESC,customer_id;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to prepare a status report. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

For every order, show its number and two separate totals of order-item amount: one for order items marked Completed and one for those marked Failed. Other statuses contribute to neither total. Show zero when no order items exist in a status. Arrange the list by order number, smallest first.

answer_sql: SELECT r.order_id,SUM(CASE WHEN e.status='Completed' THEN e.amount ELSE 0 END) AS completed_amount,SUM(CASE WHEN e.status='Failed' THEN e.amount ELSE 0 END) AS failed_amount FROM orders r LEFT JOIN order_items e ON r.order_id=e.order_id GROUP BY r.order_id ORDER BY r.order_id;

Count the order items recorded in each calendar month, including all types and statuses. Show each month and count in date order. Only months with recorded order items need to appear.

For every order, show its number and most recent recorded order item date. Include all order item statuses. Leave the date empty when no dated activity is available. Arrange the list by order number, smallest first.

solution_approach: I will left join order items to orders, group by order id and take the maximum item date.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT r.order_id,MAX(e.item_date) AS latest_event_date FROM orders r LEFT JOIN order_items e ON r.order_id=e.order_id GROUP BY r.order_id ORDER BY r.order_id;

schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)

business_scenario:

Count orders for each combination of customer group and order status. Show the group, status and count, keeping different combinations separate. Include only combinations that occur. Arrange by group and then status alphabetically.

solution_approach: I will join customers and orders and group counts by segment and status.

business_scenario:

For each customer with order items, add the order-item amount across all their orders. Show the customer number, name, total and rank, largest total first. How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will join customers, orders and order items and total event amounts per customers. I will rank the totals from highest to lowest.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: WITH totals AS (SELECT m.customer_id,m.customer_name,SUM(e.amount) total_amount FROM customers m JOIN orders r ON m.customer_id=r.customer_id JOIN order_items e ON r.order_id=e.order_id GROUP BY m.customer_id,m.customer_name) SELECT customer_id,customer_name,total_amount,RANK() OVER(ORDER BY total_amount DESC) AS amount_rank FROM totals ORDER BY amount_rank,customer_id;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to check which records need attention. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

Find orders whose most recent order item date is before 1 January 2026, or that have no recorded order item date. Show the order number and latest date, leaving it empty when unavailable. A latest date on 1 January does not qualify. Include all activity statuses. Arrange the list by order number, smallest first.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will left join order items to orders using order id so orders without activity remain. I will group each orders by order id and use HAVING on its latest item date.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT r.order_id,MAX(e.item_date) AS latest_event_date FROM orders r LEFT JOIN order_items e ON r.order_id=e.order_id GROUP BY r.order_id HAVING MAX(e.item_date)<DATE '2026-01-01' OR MAX(e.item_date) IS NULL ORDER BY r.order_id;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to compare recorded totals. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

Add the order total across each customer's orders. Find the average of these person-level totals, giving each customer equal weight and excluding customers without orders. Show the customer number and total only when above this average, largest totals first. Exclude equal totals and include all order statuses.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will use a CTE to total order total by customer id in orders. I will keep customers totals above the average total.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: WITH totals AS (SELECT customer_id,SUM(order_total) total_amount FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT customer_id,total_amount FROM totals WHERE total_amount>(SELECT AVG(total_amount) FROM totals) ORDER BY total_amount DESC;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to organize a review list. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

Show each order number, order total and group. Use High for 100,000 or more, Medium for 50,000 up to but below 100,000, and Low for values below 50,000. Under the existing exercise rule, a missing value also falls into Low. Arrange the list by order number, smallest first.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will classify orders using CASE with 100000 and 50000 order total boundaries.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT order_id,order_total,CASE WHEN order_total>=100000 THEN 'High' WHEN order_total>=50000 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Low' END amount_band FROM orders ORDER BY order_id;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to compare activity amounts. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

For each order and calendar month with order items, add the order-item amount. Show the order number, month, total and total for its previous month with recorded activity. Skip empty months: if February has none, compare March with January. Leave the previous total empty for the first available month. Arrange by order number and then month. Include all order item types and statuses and use the values as recorded.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will total event amounts in order items by order id and month in a CTE. I will use LAG partitioned by order id and ordered by event month.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: WITH monthly AS (SELECT order_id,DATE_TRUNC('month',item_date)::date event_month,SUM(amount) monthly_amount FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id,DATE_TRUNC('month',item_date)) SELECT order_id,event_month,monthly_amount,LAG(monthly_amount) OVER(PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY event_month) previous_month_amount FROM monthly ORDER BY order_id,event_month;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to prepare a progress summary. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

For each order, follow its order items in date order, using the smaller order item number first when dates match. Beside each order item, show the total order-item amount accumulated so far, including that order item. Show the order number, order item number, date, value and running total. Arrange by order number and that activity sequence. Include all order item types and statuses and use the values as recorded.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will use a windowed SUM of amount in order items partitioned by order id and ordered by item date and order item id.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT order_id,order_item_id,item_date,amount,SUM(amount) OVER(PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY item_date,order_item_id) running_amount FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id,item_date,order_item_id;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to review the largest values. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

For each order with order items, select up to two with the largest order-item amount. When values tie, choose the smaller order item number first. Show the order item number, order number and value. If only one exists, show it. Arrange by order number, then selected value highest first. Include all order item types and statuses and use the values as recorded.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will assign row numbers within each order id in order items by descending amount. I will keep row numbers 1 and 2 for every order id.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: WITH ranked AS (SELECT e.*,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY amount DESC,order_item_id) rn FROM order_items e) SELECT order_item_id,order_id,amount FROM ranked WHERE rn<=2 ORDER BY order_id,rn;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to understand the contribution of each record. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

For every order, total the order-item amount from its order items, using zero if no value is available. Show the order number, total and its percentage of the combined total across all orders. Round percentages to two decimal places; leave them empty if the combined total is zero. Include all order item types and statuses and use the values as recorded. Arrange the list by order number, smallest first.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will join orders and order items to total amounts for each orders in a CTE. I will divide each orders total by the windowed grand total.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: WITH totals AS (SELECT r.order_id,COALESCE(SUM(e.amount),0) total_amount FROM orders r LEFT JOIN order_items e ON r.order_id=e.order_id GROUP BY r.order_id) SELECT order_id,total_amount,ROUND(100.0*total_amount/NULLIF(SUM(total_amount) OVER(),0),2) percent_of_total FROM totals ORDER BY order_id;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to compare values within related groups. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

Within each customer's orders, rank the order total highest first. Equal values share a rank and the next different value gets the next number, for example 1, 2, 2, 3. Show the customer number, order number, order total and rank. Arrange by customer number, rank and then order number. Include all statuses.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will dense rank orders within each customer id by descending order total.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT customer_id,order_id,order_total,DENSE_RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_total DESC) amount_rank FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id,amount_rank,order_id;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to compare the recorded values. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

For each order, follow order items by date and then by order item number when dates match. Show its number, each order item number, date, order-item amount, and the previous order item's value for that same order. Leave the previous value empty for the first order item. Arrange by order number and that sequence. Include all order item types and statuses and use the values as recorded.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will use LAG in order items partitioned by order id ordered by item date and order item id.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT order_id,order_item_id,item_date,amount,LAG(amount) OVER(PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY item_date,order_item_id) previous_amount FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id,item_date,order_item_id;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to review the sequence of activity. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

Follow each order's order items by date, using the smaller order item number first when dates match. At each step, average the current order-item amount and the previous two recorded values in that sequence. For the first two steps, use only the activities available so far; missing values do not count toward the average. Show the order number, order item number, date, value and average. Arrange by order number and that sequence. Include all order item types and statuses and use the values as recorded.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will average the current and two preceding amounts in order items partitioned by order id ordered by item date and order item id.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT order_id,order_item_id,item_date,amount,AVG(amount) OVER(PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY item_date,order_item_id ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) moving_average FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id,item_date,order_item_id;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to prepare a status report. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

Show the number and name of each customer who has at least one order and none marked with a status other than Active. Under the existing exercise rule, a missing status does not disqualify the customer. Exclude customers with no orders. Arrange by customer number.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will use EXISTS to require that each customers has at least one orders. I will use NOT EXISTS to exclude customers with a non-Active orders.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT m.customer_id,m.customer_name FROM customers m WHERE EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM orders r WHERE r.customer_id=m.customer_id) AND NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM orders r WHERE r.customer_id=m.customer_id AND r.status<>'Active') ORDER BY m.customer_id;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to compare results across groups. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

For each order, compare its order total with the average order total of orders sharing its status. Show its number, status and order total only when above that average. Include the order itself when calculating its group's average; exclude equal values. Arrange by status alphabetically and then order total, highest first.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will compare each orders with the average order total for its own status.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT order_id,status,order_total FROM orders r WHERE order_total>(SELECT AVG(x.order_total) FROM orders x WHERE x.status=r.status) ORDER BY status,order_total DESC;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to check the recorded history. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

For every order with order items, show its number, earliest order item date, latest order item date and elapsed calendar days between them. The same first and last date gives zero days. Omit orders without order items. Include all activity statuses. Arrange the list by order number, smallest first.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will join orders and order items, group by order id and take minimum and maximum item date. I will subtract the first date from the last date to get active days.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT r.order_id,MIN(e.item_date) first_event,MAX(e.item_date) last_event,MAX(e.item_date)-MIN(e.item_date) active_days FROM orders r JOIN order_items e ON r.order_id=e.order_id GROUP BY r.order_id ORDER BY r.order_id;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to review how activity is distributed. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

For every order item, show its number, linked order number, order-item amount and percentage contribution to that order's total order-item amount. Round percentages to two decimal places; leave the percentage empty when the total is zero. Arrange by order number and then order item number. Include all order item types and statuses and use the values as recorded.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will divide each order items amount by the total amount within its order id partition.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT order_item_id,order_id,amount,ROUND(100.0*amount/NULLIF(SUM(amount) OVER(PARTITION BY order_id),0),2) record_percent FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id,order_item_id;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to prepare a summary for each group. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

Add the order total across each customer's orders, including all statuses. Within each customer group, select the one with the largest total. Break ties by choosing the smaller customer number. Show their number, name, group and total. Exclude customers without orders, and arrange the groups alphabetically.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will join customers and orders to total order total for every customers and segment. I will row-number within each segment and keep rank 1.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: WITH totals AS (SELECT m.customer_id,m.customer_name,m.segment,SUM(r.order_total) total_amount FROM customers m JOIN orders r ON m.customer_id=r.customer_id GROUP BY m.customer_id,m.customer_name,m.segment), ranked AS (SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY segment ORDER BY total_amount DESC,customer_id) rn FROM totals) SELECT customer_id,customer_name,segment,total_amount FROM ranked WHERE rn=1 ORDER BY segment;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to identify records needing a closer look. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

Find order items whose order-item amount is above the average for all order items belonging to the same order. Include the current order item when calculating that average. Show the order item number, order number and value. Exclude values equal to the average. Arrange by order number and then value highest first. Include all order item types and statuses and use the values as recorded.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will compare each order items amount with the average amount for its parent order id.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT order_item_id,order_id,amount FROM order_items e WHERE amount>(SELECT AVG(x.amount) FROM order_items x WHERE x.order_id=e.order_id) ORDER BY order_id,amount DESC;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to review the people represented in the records. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

Count the orders belonging to every registered customer, including zero for those with none. Average those counts, giving each customer equal weight. Show the number, name and count for customers above that average. Include all order statuses. Sort by count highest first, using the smaller customer number first for ties.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will left join customers and orders and count orders for every customers in a CTE. I will keep customers counts above the average master count.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: WITH counts AS (SELECT m.customer_id,m.customer_name,COUNT(r.order_id) record_count FROM customers m LEFT JOIN orders r ON m.customer_id=r.customer_id GROUP BY m.customer_id,m.customer_name) SELECT customer_id,customer_name,record_count FROM counts WHERE record_count>(SELECT AVG(record_count) FROM counts) ORDER BY record_count DESC,customer_id;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to compare activity across categories. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

For every order, show its number and separate totals of order-item amount for order items marked Completed, Pending and Failed. Other statuses contribute to none of these totals. Show zero for a status with no order items. Arrange the list by order number, smallest first.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will join orders and order items to conditionally sum Completed, Pending and Failed event amounts per orders.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: SELECT r.order_id,SUM(CASE WHEN e.status='Completed' THEN e.amount ELSE 0 END) completed_amount,SUM(CASE WHEN e.status='Pending' THEN e.amount ELSE 0 END) pending_amount,SUM(CASE WHEN e.status='Failed' THEN e.amount ELSE 0 END) failed_amount FROM orders r LEFT JOIN order_items e ON r.order_id=e.order_id GROUP BY r.order_id ORDER BY r.order_id;

business_scenario:
A store manager wants to prepare an up-to-date review. The team has records of customers, orders and order items.

For each order with order items, select the one with the latest date. If several share that date, select the largest order item number. Show its order item number, order number, date, type, order-item amount and status. Include all activity statuses and omit orders without activity. Arrange the list by order number, smallest first.

How would you prepare this information? Explain your approach in your own words. You do not need to write SQL.
solution_approach: I will row number order items partitioned by order id from newest to oldest by item date and order item id. I will keep row number 1 as the latest event.
schema: customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, city, segment, joined_date); products(product_id PK, product_name, category, status, base_value); orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, order_date, status, order_total); order_items(order_item_id PK, order_id FK, item_date, item_type, quantity, amount, status)
answer_sql: WITH ranked AS (SELECT e.*,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY item_date DESC,order_item_id DESC) rn FROM order_items e) SELECT order_item_id,order_id,item_date,item_type,amount,status FROM ranked WHERE rn=1 ORDER BY order_id;
